pr.body:
One potential problem we have with batch processing is that any one slow item will clog up the whole batch. This pr implements a queueing method instead, where we keep N queues that each have their own workers. There's still a chance of individual items backlogging a queue, but we can try increased concurrency here to reduce the chances of that happening

<!-- Describe your PR here. -->
pr.title: feat(uptime): Add ability to use queues to manage parallelism

raw_findings.body: Each queue is created with no maxsize, so it grows without bound; the offset_tracker sets also grow, so a single slow group causes unbounded memory growth (potential OOM) instead of the 'natural backpressure' the class docstring claims.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Runtime memory usage grows without limit under load; the documented backpressure guarantee is false.
raw_findings.impact: Each queue is created with no maxsize, so it grows without bound; the offset_tracker sets also grow, so a single slow group causes unbounded memory growth (potential OOM) instead of the 'natural backpressure' the class docstring claims.
raw_findings.root_cause: Work queues are instantiated with unlimited capacity and submit() unconditionally accepts messages, so no flow control exists.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Bound the queues (queue.Queue(maxsize=...)) and translate a full queue in submit() into arroyo backpressure (raise MessageRejected) rather than silently buffering, or otherwise implement real backpressure; update the docstring accordingly.
raw_findings.title: Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure and can exhaust memory
raw_findings.trigger: A group whose result_processor is slow (the exact scenario this PR targets) keeps receiving messages faster than its single worker drains them, while arroyo continues delivering via SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit, which never raises MessageRejected.

raw_findings.body: Items still queued at shutdown are never processed despite the immediate=False (drain) request, so their offsets are never completed/committed and they are reprocessed on restart, duplicating side effects (e.g. duplicate snuba/eap production).
raw_findings.failure_mode: Graceful-shutdown drain silently no-ops, increasing duplicate processing.
raw_findings.impact: Items still queued at shutdown are never processed despite the immediate=False (drain) request, so their offsets are never completed/committed and they are reprocessed on restart, duplicating side effects (e.g. duplicate snuba/eap production).
raw_findings.root_cause: The worker loop guard and the shutdown ordering both stop the worker before the intended graceful drain can occur.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Do not set worker.shutdown before draining; rely solely on queue.shutdown(immediate=False) plus the queue.ShutDown exception to terminate, so remaining items are drained before workers exit.
raw_findings.title: Setting worker.shutdown before draining defeats immediate=False graceful drain
raw_findings.trigger: shutdown() sets every worker.shutdown = True first and only afterwards calls q.shutdown(immediate=False); a worker that finishes its current item re-evaluates the loop condition and exits even though queued items remain.

raw_findings.body: close() shuts down the shared queue_pool's workers and queues, but the factory does not recreate it, so the next SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy submits to already-shut-down queues, causing queue.ShutDown errors and dropped/uncommitted messages after rebalance.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Post-rebalance message processing fails because it targets a dead queue pool.
raw_findings.impact: close() shuts down the shared queue_pool's workers and queues, but the factory does not recreate it, so the next SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy submits to already-shut-down queues, causing queue.ShutDown errors and dropped/uncommitted messages after rebalance.
raw_findings.root_cause: A single long-lived queue_pool created in the factory __init__ is torn down by per-assignment strategy close().
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Own the queue_pool lifecycle at the strategy level (create a fresh pool per create_with_partitions) or have the factory recreate the pool after a strategy close, so a closed pool is never reused.
raw_findings.title: Strategy.close() shuts down the factory-owned queue_pool that is reused across partition assignments
raw_findings.trigger: A partition rebalance causes arroyo to close the current strategy (calling close()), then call create_with_partitions again for the new assignment; the factory still holds the same FixedQueuePool created once in __init__.

raw_findings.body: The assertion only passes because the 1s commit loop has not yet fired, making the test timing-dependent/flaky, and it documents behavior (errors block commits) that the code does not actually implement.
raw_findings.evidence: assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets
raw_findings.failure_mode: Flaky/misleading test that can pass or fail based on scheduling and misrepresents error handling.
raw_findings.impact: The assertion only passes because the 1s commit loop has not yet fired, making the test timing-dependent/flaky, and it documents behavior (errors block commits) that the code does not actually implement.
raw_findings.root_cause: The test expectation contradicts the finally-based unconditional complete_offset and relies on commit-loop timing.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Align the test with actual semantics: either assert the failed offset IS eventually committed (at-least-once) after waiting for the commit loop, or change the implementation to skip completing offsets on processing failure and then assert accordingly.
raw_findings.title: Error-handling test asserts no commit but implementation completes failed offsets
raw_findings.trigger: The worker's finally block calls complete_offset() even when result_processor raises, so both offsets 100 and 101 become committable; the commit loop runs on a 1s timer while the test breaks ~0.2s after processing.
